input.strategy_title: AMD GPU (ROCm) enablement for serving and training
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Two strategic customers are standardizing on AMD Instinct accelerators and need
RHOAI to serve and train on ROCm. Upstream vLLM and PyTorch both publish ROCm
support, but the platform ships only CUDA runtime builds, and we have no
first-hand data on functional or performance parity for our supported model
set. Feature and performance validation requires physical AMD GPU hardware —
none exists in our CI fleet today — and upstream ROCm image cadence is
controlled by AMD and the upstream communities.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | A validation campaign on physical AMD Instinct hardware establishes functional and performance parity data for vLLM serving of the supported model set, producing the go/no-go scope for productization. |
| HLR-2 | P0 | A supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime is productized for the models the validation campaign clears. |
| HLR-3 | P1 | PyTorch training on ROCm is supported for single- and multi-GPU jobs admitted through Kueue, with amd.com/gpu quota handling. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | Documentation states supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites, and the validated model list. |

## Affected Components

- KServe
- Serving Runtimes
- Training Operator
- Distributed Workloads

## Out of Scope

- Intel Gaudi or other non-AMD accelerator families
- AMD GPU sharing/partitioning support

## Open Questions

1. Hardware access: the validation campaign (HLR-1) needs dedicated AMD
   Instinct nodes — procurement or partner-lab access is unresolved.
2. Upstream ROCm build cadence: whether AMD's runtime image releases align
   with our release trains is outside our control.

# AMD Instinct validation campaign for vLLM ROCm serving parity

## Description

Runs a validation campaign on physical AMD Instinct accelerators to establish
functional and performance parity data for vLLM serving of the platform's supported
model set, and produces the go/no-go scope that determines which models the
productized ROCm serving runtime will support. This resolves the strategy's core
unknown — the platform ships only CUDA runtime builds and has no first-hand ROCm
parity data for its supported models.

## Scope

- Define the campaign protocol: enumerate the supported model set, define per-model
  functional pass/fail criteria, and define the performance parity measurement
  methodology (throughput and latency on AMD Instinct versus the productized CUDA
  baseline).
- Establish the hardware access arrangement required to execute the campaign —
  procurement of dedicated AMD Instinct nodes or a partner-lab engagement (the
  strategy flags this access as unresolved).
- Execute the campaign: serve each supported model with vLLM ROCm builds on AMD
  Instinct hardware, collecting functional results and performance measurements.
- Produce the validation report: per-model functional and performance results, a
  go/no-go recommendation stating the cleared model scope for productization, and
  root-cause notes for models that fail or underperform.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The validation report covers every model in the supported model set, recording a
  functional pass/fail result and performance measurements against the CUDA baseline
  for each model.
- The report states a go/no-go recommendation with an explicit list of cleared
  models, traceable to the per-model results.
- Models that fail functional validation or miss performance parity are documented
  with root-cause detail sufficient to scope any follow-up work.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): the validation campaign and the go/no-go scope for productization are
  this epic's entire deliverable.

## Risks and Notes

- Hardware access is an availability precondition controlled by parties outside the
  strategy (procurement, partner labs); no AMD Instinct nodes exist in the CI fleet
  today. The epic's work includes securing the arrangement, but the granting of
  access and its turnaround are not conditions this epic's deliverable produces —
  campaign start is exposed to their timing.
- The campaign consumes upstream vLLM ROCm builds whose release cadence is
  controlled by AMD; the campaign protocol should pin image versions explicitly.

# Productize a supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime for validated models

## Description

Productizes a supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime for the models cleared by the AMD
Instinct validation campaign, built and released through the existing runtime
productization pipeline alongside the CUDA builds. The scope of supported models is
set by the campaign's go/no-go outcome; the engineering approach mirrors the existing
CUDA vLLM runtime productization.

## Scope

- Build and release a vLLM ROCm runtime image for the platform version in the
  midstream vLLM repo, mirroring the existing CUDA runtime image productization.
- Ship a ServingRuntime/ClusterServingRuntime definition that deploys the ROCm
  runtime with AMD GPU resource requests so KServe InferenceServices can use it.
  KServe itself requires no code changes — it is accelerator-agnostic — so
  validating that InferenceServices schedule and serve correctly on AMD Instinct
  nodes is part of this epic.
- Pin an upstream ROCm base image release that is compatible with the platform
  release train, and record the compatibility choice.
- Verify end-to-end serving on AMD Instinct nodes for the cleared model set.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The vLLM ROCm runtime image builds green in the platform build pipeline and is
  released for the platform version.
- A ServingRuntime definition deploying the ROCm runtime is available, and KServe
  InferenceServices using it schedule onto AMD Instinct nodes and serve inference
  requests for every model cleared by the validation campaign.
- The runtime pins a released upstream ROCm base image compatible with the platform
  release, and the pinning is recorded.
- Existing CUDA-based runtime images and ServingRuntime definitions are unaffected
  (no regression to the currently supported serving paths).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0): a supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime productized for the models the
  validation campaign clears.

## Risks and Notes

- Upstream ROCm image release cadence is controlled by AMD and may not align with
  the platform release trains; the mitigation is pinning whichever released upstream
  image is compatible, and re-pinning per release. This timing risk is externally
  controlled and cannot be compressed.
- The model scope of this epic is determined by the validation campaign outcome; a
  partial pass rescopes the epic to the cleared subset, and a full no-go descopes
  the productization work entirely.

# PyTorch ROCm training support in the Training Operator

## Description

Enables PyTorch training on ROCm so that single-GPU and multi-GPU (distributed)
PyTorchJob workloads run on AMD Instinct nodes through the Training Operator,
mirroring the existing NVIDIA GPU training support.

## Scope

- Enable PyTorchJob execution on ROCm-enabled nodes: PyTorch ROCm training images
  and job specifications that request AMD GPU resources for single-GPU and
  multi-GPU distributed topologies.
- Validate functional training runs on AMD Instinct hardware for single- and
  multi-GPU PyTorchJob workloads, including jobs whose admission goes through the
  platform's queueing layer with AMD GPU quota.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Single-GPU PyTorchJob workloads requesting AMD GPU resources run to completion on
  ROCm-enabled nodes with correct training results.
- Multi-GPU distributed PyTorchJob workloads requesting AMD GPU resources run to
  completion on ROCm-enabled nodes.
- Existing NVIDIA-based PyTorchJob behavior is unaffected.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1): PyTorch training on ROCm supported for single- and multi-GPU jobs —
  the job-execution half; queue admission and amd.com/gpu quota handling are covered
  by the Kueue quota work on the Distributed Workloads component.

## Risks and Notes

- Functional validation requires physical AMD Instinct hardware, which is not yet
  in the CI fleet; access is being arranged through the serving validation
  campaign's hardware work and remains a shared availability risk.
- PyTorch ROCm training images depend on upstream PyTorch/AMD ROCm releases whose
  cadence is externally controlled.

# Kueue quota handling for AMD GPU (amd.com/gpu) resources

## Description

Extends the Distributed Workloads queueing layer so that workloads requesting AMD
GPU resources (`amd.com/gpu`) are admitted through Kueue with correct quota
handling, providing the admission path for ROCm training jobs. This covers the
queueing and quota half of ROCm training support; PyTorchJob execution itself is
handled by the Training Operator work.

## Scope

- Support `amd.com/gpu` in the Kueue quota model: ClusterQueue/LocalQueue resource
  flavors covering AMD GPU resources so workloads requesting them are admitted
  under quota with all-or-nothing (gang) admission semantics.
- Validate quota accounting and admission for multi-GPU PyTorchJob workloads
  requesting `amd.com/gpu`, including enforcement of quota limits.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Workloads requesting `amd.com/gpu` are admitted through Kueue quota
  (ClusterQueue/LocalQueue) and run to completion, including multi-GPU PyTorchJob
  topologies.
- Quota limits on `amd.com/gpu` are enforced: a workload whose request exceeds its
  queue's quota remains pending rather than being partially admitted.
- Existing NVIDIA GPU (`nvidia.com/gpu`) quota handling and queue behavior are
  unaffected.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1): PyTorch training on ROCm for jobs admitted through Kueue with
  amd.com/gpu quota handling — the queue-admission and quota half.

## Risks and Notes

- End-to-end admission validation on real hardware benefits from AMD Instinct node
  access (shared availability risk with the rest of the strategy); admission and
  quota semantics can otherwise be exercised with fake/simulated resource flavors.

# Document AMD GPU (ROCm) support for serving and training

## Description

Authors and publishes the platform documentation for AMD GPU (ROCm) support,
stating the supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites, and the validated model
list, and describing the ROCm serving and training capabilities delivered by this
strategy.

## Scope

Content outline:

- Supported AMD Instinct hardware: the accelerator models/configurations validated
  by the campaign.
- Driver and node prerequisites for AMD GPU nodes.
- The validated model list for the vLLM ROCm serving runtime, matching the
  validation campaign results and the productized runtime's scope.
- Using ROCm training: submitting single- and multi-GPU PyTorchJobs and requesting
  `amd.com/gpu` quota through the platform's queueing layer.
- Scope boundaries carried from the strategy: non-AMD accelerator families and AMD
  GPU sharing/partitioning are not supported.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Published documentation states the supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites,
  and the validated model list, consistent with the validation campaign results and
  the productized ROCm serving runtime and training support.
- The content is technically reviewed against the implementations by the owning
  engineering teams before publication.
- The documentation is available in the platform release in which the ROCm support
  ships.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P2): documentation stating supported AMD hardware, driver prerequisites,
  and the validated model list.

# AMD GPU (ROCm) enablement for serving and training — Decomposition

Strategy RHAISTRAT-9020 (priority: Major) enables AMD Instinct (ROCm) accelerators
for vLLM serving and PyTorch training. All four strategy components (KServe, Serving
Runtimes, Training Operator, Distributed Workloads) have architecture-context files —
no onboarding chains are needed. The strategy carries two explicit open questions
(hardware access, upstream ROCm image cadence), which are handled as noted below.

## Epic List

| ID | Title | Type | Team | Priority |
|----|-------|------|------|----------|
| RHAISTRAT-9020-E001 | AMD Instinct validation campaign for vLLM ROCm serving parity | Investigation | RHOAI Serving | P0 |
| RHAISTRAT-9020-E002 | Productize a supported vLLM ROCm serving runtime for validated models | Implementation | RHOAI Serving | P0 |
| RHAISTRAT-9020-E003 | PyTorch ROCm training support in the Training Operator | Implementation | Distributed Workloads | P1 |
| RHAISTRAT-9020-E004 | Kueue quota handling for AMD GPU (amd.com/gpu) resources | Implementation | Distributed Workloads | P1 |
| RHAISTRAT-9020-E005 | Document AMD GPU (ROCm) support for serving and training | Implementation (docs-authoring) | RHOAI Documentation | P1 |

## Dependency DAG

```mermaid
graph TD
    E001["E001 validation campaign (Investigation)"] --> E002["E002 ROCm serving runtime productization"]
    E001 --> E005["E005 documentation"]
    E002 --> E005
    E003["E003 PyTorch ROCm training"] --> E005
    E004["E004 Kueue amd.com/gpu quota"] --> E005
```

## DAG Justification

| Edge | Rule | Rationale |
|------|------|-----------|
| E001 → E002 | Rule 3 (Investigation gates downstream) | HLR-2 scopes the productized runtime to "the models the validation campaign clears" — the campaign outcome is a true gate (`rewrite`: rescope to the cleared model set; a full no-go descopes productization). Recorded as `gated_by` on E002. |
| E001 → E005 | Rule 11 + content dependency | HLR-4 requires docs to state the validated model list, which is the campaign's direct deliverable. |
| E002 → E005 | Rule 11 (docs last) | Documentation describes the productized runtime. |
| E003 → E005 | Rule 11 (docs last) | Documentation describes the delivered training support. |
| E004 → E005 | Rule 11 (docs last) | Documentation describes the delivered quota handling. |
| no edge E001 ∥ E003, E004 | Rule 14 (independent repos) | The campaign validates vLLM serving only (HLR-1); the training track (Training Operator, Kueue) proceeds independently in separate repos. |
| no edge E003 ∥ E004 | Rules 14/15 | Training Operator and Kueue are separate components/repos with no shared build artifact; the runtime integration (PyTorchJobs admitted under amd.com/gpu quota) is verified by each epic's acceptance criteria, not by a DAG edge. |

Conditional branches: the campaign's outcomes are bounded (full pass / partial pass /
no-go) but they change only the model-set scope of the single downstream productization
epic, not which epics exist or how the DAG is structured — E002 covers "the models the
campaign clears" under every outcome. The gate is therefore expressed as
`gate_failure_impact` on E002 rather than as branch epic files.

## HLR Traceability Matrix

| HLR | Priority | Epic(s) |
|-----|----------|---------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | RHAISTRAT-9020-E001 |
| HLR-2 | P0 | RHAISTRAT-9020-E002 |
| HLR-3 | P1 | RHAISTRAT-9020-E003, RHAISTRAT-9020-E004 |
| HLR-4 | P2 | RHAISTRAT-9020-E005 |

All four HLRs are covered; no orphaned requirements. HLR-3 spans two components
(Training Operator, Distributed Workloads) owned by the same team, so it maps to two
epics per the component-boundary rule — the split is architectural (job execution vs
queue admission/quota), not priority-based.

## Component Mapping Notes

- **KServe — passive component.** The strategy lists KServe as affected but describes
  no change to it, and the architecture context (`kserve.md`) shows KServe as the
  accelerator-agnostic lifecycle/routing layer over ServingRuntime CRDs. The ROCm work
  lives in the runtime images and ServingRuntime definitions. KServe validation
  (InferenceServices scheduling onto AMD Instinct nodes) is an acceptance criterion on
  E002, the nearest active epic — same owning team (RHOAI Serving), so no separate
  validation epic is generated.
- **E001 component.** The campaign validates vLLM serving, so it is filed under the
  canonical component `Serving Runtimes` (closest canonical name for the vLLM runtime
  work it gates).
- **E005 component.** Documentation work is filed under the canonical component
  `Documentation`.
- All components are present in `.context/architecture-context/` — no new-component
  onboarding chains (Rule 20) apply. The ROCm runtime image is a new image variant in
  the already-Konflux-onboarded vLLM midstream repo, so it is handled inside E002's
  scope rather than as a separate onboarding epic.

## Health Warnings

- **Missing strategy sections.** The strategy has no Impacted Teams table, no
  Dependencies table, no Given/When/Then Acceptance Criteria, and no Non-Functional
  Requirements. Teams were inferred from the architecture-context owning-team fields
  (KServe and Serving Runtimes → RHOAI Serving; Training Operator and Distributed
  Workloads → Distributed Workloads). Per-epic acceptance criteria were derived from
  the HLRs.
- **Hardware availability precondition (non-blocking).** No AMD Instinct nodes exist
  in the CI fleet, and procurement/partner-lab access is unresolved (strategy open
  question 1). Access being granted is externally controlled and is NOT an acceptance
  criterion anywhere; E001's scope includes *securing* the arrangement, and the AC sits
  on the validated report. The same hardware constraint affects the functional
  validation ACs on E003 and E004 — shared risk, tracked in each epic's Risks.
- **Upstream ROCm image cadence (non-blocking).** AMD controls ROCm runtime image
  release timing (strategy open question 2). Modeled as a precondition with tiered
  delivery (below), not as a separate epic: the productization epic pins a released
  upstream ROCm base image compatible with the platform release train. Schedule impact
  from upstream timing cannot be compressed by this decomposition.
- **Docs priority note (not an inversion).** HLR-4 is P2, but the docs-authoring epic
